name: Gaulish / gaulois
confidence_why: Gaulish stress is known only from Gallo-Romance place-name reflexes, and d'Arbois de Jubainville 1908, Dottin 1918 and Lambert 1994 all read the un-Latin antepenultimate forms (Nîmes, Bourges, Dreux, Troyes) as the genuine Gaulish accent with the penultimate doublets (Nemours, Berry) as Latin-type or later, while Wolf 1982 accepts long-penult proparoxytones but says no accent rule can be established and Falc'hun 1963 alone argues both accentuations were Gaulish, so we defend antepenultimate stress rather than the catalogue's 'variable', on a thin reconstruction with one dissenter.

catalog_quote: Dans les langues celtiques insulaires, l'accent principal est sur l'initiale, mais il y a des traces d'un accent plus ancien et plus mobile, analogue à celui de plusieurs autres langues indo-européennes. L'accent gaulois ne nous est connu qu'à 1 époque romane par des noms de lieux qui ont persisté en français en gardant leur ancien accent, et cet accent n'est pas conforme aux lois de l'accentuation latine. Il pouvait porter sur l'antépénultième, même si la pénultième était longue. D'après leHet qu'il a eu sur les voyelles atones, cet accent était un accent d intensité. new_statements.translation: In the Insular Celtic languages the main accent is on the initial syllable, but there are traces of an older and more mobile accent [...]. The Gaulish accent is known to us only from the Romance period, through place names that survived in French keeping their old accent, and this accent does not conform to the laws of Latin accentuation. It could fall on the antepenult even when the penult was long. Judging from its effect on unstressed vowels, this accent was an intensity (stress) accent. It falls on the initial syllable in the following derivatives and compounds: Nemausum Nîmes, Arelate Arles, Condate Candes, Brivate Brioude, Mimate Mende, Tricasses Troyes. It falls on the last syllable of the first member in the following compounds: Eburovices Evreux, Viducasses Vieux, Durocasses Dreux, Bodiocasses Bayeux, Bituriges Bourges, Caturiges Chorges, Autessiodurum Auxerre, [Epo]manduodurum Mandeure, Balodurum Balleure.

new_statements.rule_in_words: A reconstructed intensity (stress) accent, known only from the French reflexes of Gaulish place names; explicitly not the Latin weight rule, since it could stand on the antepenult even over a long penult. Dottin states the placement morphologically (initial syllable in derivatives/trisyllabic compounds; last syllable of the first member in longer compounds), but every archaic reflex he lists is antepenult-stressed (Némausus, Árelate, Cóndate, Brívate, Mímate, Trícasses; Eburóvices, Vidúcasses, Durócasses, Bodiócasses, Bitúriges, Catúriges, Autessiódurum, Epomandúodurum, Balódurum), so the placement his data support is antepenultimate, quantity-insensitive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Dottin posits an earlier pitch accent ('antérieurement à l'accent d'intensité, il y avait un accent de hauteur, sur lequel nous n'avons aucun renseignement', p.104) about which nothing is known; Greek-transcription accents are dismissed as following Greek accent laws.
new_statements.exceptions: p.104: analogy produced, beside the old forms, new names conforming to Latin accent laws (Nemours beside Nîmes, as Lemausum > Limours; Arlet beside Arles; Condé beside Candes; Brivé beside Brioude; Mimat beside Mende), and some names show movement of the accent off the initial (Belisama > Blismes, Blesmes, Bellême). p.61 n.2: several vowel losses may have been produced by an intensity accent. pp.307-308 (Conclusion): 'L'accent tonique ne semble pas avoir eu d'action sur le vocalisme ou sur le consonantisme', which tempers the intensity-accent inference.
new_statements.identity_note: Dottin 1918 describes continental (Transalpine) Gaulish as a whole, reconstructed from Gallo-Roman place names surviving in French; no dialect is singled out. The Insular Celtic initial-accent remark in the same paragraph is about Irish/Brittonic, not Gaulish.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The works list contained a single work (Dottin 1918), which was opened, so there were no silent or not-opened listed works to spot-check. As a courtesy the in-folder Stifter 2008 Old Celtic handouts (6 Gaulish A, 7 Gaulish B; not in the works list) were re-a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/Betonung/tonic: no Gaulish accent content (the single hit, line 237 of A, concerns a Greek dialect), confirming the compilers note. Nothing missed in Dottin: the book index lists accent tonique only at pp.61, 103-104, 307, all read.

readall_conflicts: Within the single work opened here there is no conflict, only Dottin's own hedging (accent known solely from Romance-period toponym reflexes; Latin-type doublets treated as analogical; Conclusion says the accent seems to have had no effect on vowels or consonants, which sits awkwardly with the p.61/p.104 inference of an intensity accent from vowel loss). Against the catalog: the classification variable reads Dottin's two morphologically stated placements as competing patterns, whereas all his archaic examples are antepenult and the penult forms are explicitly Latin-analogical; the prior check notes in the same folder (d'Arbois de Jubainville 1908 'antepenult even with long penult'; Wolf 1982 'proparoxytons à pénultième longue, à l'opposé du latin' but 'on n'a pas encore pu en établir des règles'; Lambert 1994 and Falc'hun 1963 on antepenult vs penult doublets, with Falc'hun arguing the penult layer is older) are all compatible with antepenult as the non-Latin Gaulish placement, with the open question being whether the penult layer is also Gaulish.

audit.recode_to: not determinable (reconstructed from Romance reflexes of ~20 toponyms; the one generally accepted fact is antepenultimate stress even over a long penult -- Bitúriges>Bourges, Némausus>Nîmes, Bodiócasses>Bayeux -- i.e. NOT the Latin weight rule; penult-stressed doublets Berry/Nemours/Condé/Arlet are analysed as Latin analogy (d'Arbois 1908, Dottin 1920), Gallo-Roman sociolinguistic variants (Lambert 1994) or a second, chronologically distinct Gaulish accentuation (majority view per Falc'hun 1963; De Bernardo Stempel 1994/1995/2023) -- never as synchronic free variation; Wolf 1982 p.281 'on n'a pas encore pu en établir des règles'). Acceptable alternative under the catalog's Oscan/Umbrian precedent (hedged reconstructions coded fixed and weight-blind): fixed antepenultimate, quantity-insensitive, exceptions = listed penult doublets of Latin/Gallo-Roman or later-stage origin.

sources.quote: 'Nous n'avons pas beaucoup d'indices sur l'accent gaulois : quelques formes du latin de Gaule ont un comportement special. On a depuis longtemps releve les deux traitements que presentent le nom de cites gauloises : un accent antepenultieme donne Rennes, Bourges, et l'accent penultieme donne Redon, Berry. Bituriges > Bourges / Bituriges > Berry. Ainsi Nemausus donne (accent penultieme) Nemours, mais avec l'accent sur l'antepenultieme, Nimes ; Condate donne Condes ou Conde, Arelate donne Arles ou Arlet. Autres exemples de formes accentuees sur l'antepenultieme : Caturiges > Chorges, Cambo-ritum

tone.quote: Aber nach allem, was wir wissen oder richtiger gesagt was ziemlich allgemein vermutet wird, ist schon der altgallische akzent ein expiratorischer mit ausgesprochenem unterschiede zwischen betonten und tonlosen silben gewesen. Allerdings steht die annähme vielleicht auf viel schwächeren füssen, als gemeiniglich gesagt wird; [...] [p.63:] Die tonlage in einer spräche, deren flexion uns so viel wie unbekannt ist, deren Wortschatz uns fast nur unter der geötalt von zumeist nicht oder nicht sicher zu deutenden orts- und flussnamen bekannt ist, wird wol nie mit Sicherheit zu bestimmen sein.

tone.translation: But according to everything we know, or more correctly what is fairly generally supposed, already the Old Gaulish accent was an expiratory one with a pronounced difference between stressed and unstressed syllables. Admittedly the assumption perhaps stands on much weaker feet than is commonly said; [...] The accentuation of a language whose inflection is as good as unknown to us, whose vocabulary is known to us almost only in the shape of place and river names that mostly cannot, or cannot securely, be interpreted, will probably never be determined with certainty.

tone.quote: Grâce 1 leur héritage indo-européen les langues celtiques, comme le latin, connaissent des voyelles longues et brèves. Quant à l’accent, on n'a pas encore pu en établir des règles. Cependant, à la suite des travaux de Meyer-Lübke, il est admis que le gaulois possédait des proparoxytons à pénultième longue (p. ex. 3ituriges /Bourges) , I l'opposé du latin.
tone.translation: 'Thanks to their Indo-European heritage the Celtic languages, like Latin, have long and short vowels. As for the accent, no rules have yet been established for it. However, following Meyer-Lübke's work, it is accepted that Gaulish had proparoxytones with a long penult (e.g. Bituriges / Bourges), contrary to Latin.' (scanned '1' = 'à', '3ituriges' = 'Bituriges', ', I' = 'à')

tone.quote: On sait que beaucoup de noms de lieux gaulois étaient accentués de deux manières différentes, ainsi Condate et Nemausus. Condé postule Condâte, et Nemours Nemausus, mais Condes et Nîmes exigent Côndate et Nemausus. La plupart des linguistes supposent donc deux accentuations successives du gaulois, en quoi ils ont certainement raison.
tone.translation: 'It is known that many Gaulish place names were accented in two different ways, e.g. Condate and Nemausus. Condé presupposes Condáte, and Nemours Nemaúsus, but Condes and Nîmes require Cóndate and Némausus. Most linguists therefore assume two successive accentuations of Gaulish, in which they are certainly right.'

sources.citation: Haberl, Rudolf. 1912. Gallisch andera und die Betonung im Gallischen. Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 8: 233-235. doi:10.1515/zcph.1912.8.1.233. Open scan of the volume: archive.org item zeitschrift_fuer_celtische_philologie_1912_8.

tone.quote: Wie wir früher aus den Untersuchungen über die zu- sammengesetzen Ortsnamen ersehen haben, werden die gallischen Wörter bei ihrer Aufnahme ins Romanische dem lat.-rom. Be- tonungsgesetz unterworfen und gerade die Ausnahmen, in denen Zurückziehung des Akzentes eintrat, haben uns gezeigt, dafs im Gallischen der Ton auf der ersten Silbe, der Stammsilbe, ruhte.
tone.translation: As we saw earlier from the investigation of the compound place names, Gaulish words on being taken into Romance were subjected to the Latin-Romance accent law, and precisely the exceptions in which retraction of the accent occurred have shown us that in Gaulish the stress rested on the first syllable, the root syllable.

sources.citation: Haberl, Rudolf. 1912. Zur Kenntnis des Gallischen. Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie 8: 82-101 (section 8 'Die Betonung im Gallischen', pp.95-100). doi:10.1515/zcph.1912.8.1.82. Open scan of the volume: archive.org item zeitschrift_fuer_celtische_philologie_1912_8.

tone.quote: Das Ergebnis dieser Untersuchung lälst sich folgendermafsen formulieren: Im Gallischen herrschte auch in den Zu- sammensetzungen Anfangsbetonung wie im Germani- schen. Bei der Romanisierung wurden die gallischen Ortsnamen dem lateinischen Betonungsgesetze unter- worfen. Nur in einzelnen Fällen wurde ein Ausgleich mit der gallischen Betonung angestrebt; doch auch dann rückte der Akzent nicht über die drittletzte Silbe hinaus.
tone.locator: pp.99-100, end of section 8 ('folgendermafsen' sic; page break '100 RUDOLF HABERL' falls after 'Ausgleich')
tone.translation: The result of this investigation can be formulated as follows: in Gaulish, initial stress prevailed also in compounds, as in Germanic. On romanisation the Gaulish place names were subjected to the Latin accent law. Only in individual cases was a compromise with the Gaulish accentuation sought; but even then the accent did not move back beyond the antepenultimate syllable.

tone.quote: « Une loi de l'accentuation latine est que la pénultième longue est toujours accentuée ; il en était autrement en gaulois : Bodiè- casses; plus tard BadiÔcasses , Baibcasses est devenu Bayeux (Calvados); Durècasses, Dreux (Eure-et-Loir); Trîcasses, Troyes (Aube); Vidûcasses, Vieux (Calvados), dans la Gaule septentrionale. [...] « Pour les mots dont la pénultième est brève, la règle est la même en gaulois qu'en latin, c'est l'antépénultième qui est frappée par l'accent : Argentomâgus « Argenton », Carantomâgus « Cranton »
tone.locator: p.272 (opening of the communication) and p.274
tone.translation: 'A law of Latin accentuation is that a long penult is always accented; it was otherwise in Gaulish: Bodiocasses ... became Bayeux (Calvados); Durocasses, Dreux; Tricasses, Troyes; Viducasses, Vieux, in northern Gaul. [...] For words whose penult is short, the rule is the same in Gaulish as in Latin: it is the antepenult that bears the accent: Argentomagus > Argenton, Carantomagus > Cranton'
